_about: Limits of the analogy, English version of docs/limits_mars.pdf and docs/limits_moon.pdf (Ukrainian originals). Numbers are copied from the PDFs unchanged; 'verify': true marks values the PDFs themselves say must be checked against sources. Factor ids are shared between bodies where the factor is the same. site_notes[].site_id / reference_id refer to data/sites.csv.

mars.title: Limits of the analogy: Earth — Mars
mars.summary: Earth analogs are good for rehearsing field geology, drilling, cold-weather operations, searching for ice and salts, and studying dry soils. They do not replace testing in a thin CO₂ atmosphere, under space radiation and in Martian gravity.
mars.not_in_metric: Radiation, pressure and gravity are deliberately left out of the data table: no Earth analog gives a meaningful value for them. They are described here instead of in the CSV.

factors.label: Atmosphere and pressure
factors.why: Wind moves sand differently, liquid water is unstable on the surface, and equipment and materials behave differently.

factors.label: Radiation
factors.target: No global magnetic field or ozone layer; surface dose about 0.6–0.7 mSv/day according to the RAD instrument (Curiosity)
factors.earth: ≈2.4 mSv/year on average from natural sources
factors.why: Shielded shelters and limited work time are needed; this cannot be tested on Earth.
factors.verify_note: The PDF marks the RAD dose as 'to be checked'.

factors.label: Gravity
factors.why: Changes how soil, drilling, walking and loads behave.

factors.label: Temperature
factors.target: Much colder than Earth, with a daily range of tens of degrees; in polar winter the surface reaches the CO₂ frost point (about −125 °C)
factors.earth: The coldest places on Earth reach about −90 °C
factors.why: Earth has no lasting conditions this cold combined with a thin atmosphere.

factors.label: Ultraviolet
factors.target: Hard UV reaches the surface; there is no ozone layer
factors.why: Destroys organic matter on the surface; Earth deserts do not reproduce this.

factors.label: Regolith
factors.target: Fine iron-rich dust and sand; contains perchlorates (≈0.5 wt% at the Phoenix site); oxidizing and toxic
factors.earth: Soils are altered by water, wind and organisms
factors.why: Perchlorates are hazardous to equipment and people; Earth soils do not imitate this.
factors.verify_note: The PDF marks the perchlorate content at Phoenix as 'to be checked'.

factors.label: Water and ice
factors.target: Ground ice on the northern plains, hydrated minerals and traces of ancient lakes
factors.why: Earth analogs have biological processes and seasonal liquid water that Mars does not have today.

factors.label: Day and seasons
factors.target: Sol ≈24 h 40 min, year 687 Earth days, axial tilt 25.19°
factors.why: A good match, but the long Martian seasons differ.

factors.label: Dust storms
factors.target: Global storms occur that block the Sun for weeks
factors.why: They change temperature and power supply; Earth has no full analog.

mitigations.label: Pressure and atmospheric composition
mitigations.text: Low-pressure CO₂ chambers and Martian soil simulants, e.g. JSC Mars-1A.

mitigations.label: Radiation and ultraviolet
mitigations.text: Laboratory UV and irradiation sources, since Earth conditions do not reproduce them.

mitigations.label: Gravity
mitigations.text: Parabolic flights, offloading suspension rigs, water immersion.

mitigations.label: Dust and perchlorates
mitigations.text: Laboratory tests with perchlorates at safe concentrations.

mitigations.label: Isolation
mitigations.text: Closed missions such as the Mars Desert Research Station (MDRS) to test crew work and procedures.

mitigations.label: Water and ice
mitigations.text: Drilling in McMurdo permafrost as a rehearsal for work on the northern plains of Mars.

site_notes.label: Roter Kamm crater (Namibia), ≈2.5 km
site_notes.matches: Impact crater in a desert, sand-filled floor, wind erosion.
site_notes.mismatches: The target rock is granite and gneiss, not basalt; Jezero is much larger and has a delta and carbonates; much warmer; dense atmosphere.

site_notes.label: Sossusvlei red dunes
site_notes.matches: Active dunes, iron-oxide coating on the sand, wind dynamics.
site_notes.mismatches: The sand is quartz, on Mars it is basaltic; the dense atmosphere changes sand transport; fog supplies moisture.

site_notes.label: Gobabeb gravel plain
site_notes.mismatches: Lichens and fog, no craters, much warmer.

site_notes.label: Taylor and Wright Valleys (McMurdo)
site_notes.matches: Dry permafrost, salts in the soil, polygonal ground, cold.
site_notes.mismatches: In summer water melts and streams flow; pressure ~170 times higher; microbial mats; mean annual temperature about −20 °C, much warmer than Mars.

site_notes.label: Taylor and Wright Valleys (McMurdo)
site_notes.matches: Dry permafrost, salts in the soil, polygonal ground, cold.
site_notes.mismatches: In summer water melts and streams flow; pressure ~170 times higher; microbial mats; mean annual temperature about −20 °C, much warmer than Mars.

site_notes.label: Don Juan Pond (Wright Valley)
site_notes.matches: Brines and salts, an analog of Martian brines.
site_notes.mismatches: The brine is CaCl₂-based, on Mars it is perchlorates; the liquid is stable only on Earth.

site_notes.label: Beacon Valley (McMurdo)
site_notes.matches: Buried ice under a thin soil layer, sublimation polygons.
site_notes.mismatches: Dense atmosphere; the ice has a different origin.

mars.sun_note: In our data the Sun elevation for the Namib is close to 90° and matches Jezero and Gale, while in McMurdo winter the noon Sun is below the horizon, as at the Phoenix site. This is one of the best matches in the project. However, for McMurdo and Phoenix the numbers follow from latitude, not from the same climate physics.

good_for.label: Cold and dryness
good_for.text: The McMurdo Dry Valleys give realistic hyper-arid cold-desert conditions for testing equipment and sampling methods.

good_for.label: Dry permafrost and salts
good_for.text: McMurdo and Don Juan Pond allow studying soils with perchlorates and brines, important for the search for life and resources.

good_for.label: Impact structures in a desert
good_for.text: Roter Kamm shows how wind and sand change a crater over time.

good_for.label: Dunes and wind erosion
good_for.text: Namibia provides material for studying dune shapes and motion.

good_for.label: Day length
good_for.text: A Martian day is almost the same as an Earth day, so rover and crew schedules can be rehearsed in real time.

mars.conclusion: The similarity ranking shows which Earth site is closest to a Martian reference in temperature, relief, ice, composition and illumination. It does not claim that the site fully reproduces Mars. Pressure, radiation and gravity need separate test stands and chambers; combining field analogs with laboratory tests gives the most complete picture.
mars.caveat: Many numbers in the project table (temperatures, slopes, crater density, ice fraction) have status 'test'. The ranking can therefore be shown only as a demonstration of the method until they are replaced with data from MODIS, NASADEM, MOLA and the Robbins crater catalogue.

sources.label: Jezero temperatures
sources.text: Munguira et al. 2024, JGR Planets; Munguira et al. 2023

sources.label: Databases for missing values
sources.text: MOLA and Mars Trek; CRISM and REMS in PDS; MODIS LST and NASADEM in Earthdata; Robbins crater catalogue for Mars

moon.title: Limits of the analogy: Earth — Moon
moon.summary: Earth analogs are good for rehearsing logistics, drilling, cold-weather operations, searching for ice and studying impact rocks. They do not replace testing in vacuum, under space radiation and in lunar gravity.
moon.not_in_metric: Radiation, pressure and gravity are deliberately left out of the data table: no Earth analog gives a meaningful value for them. They are described here instead of in the CSV.

factors.label: Atmosphere and pressure
factors.why: No wind, fog, scattered light or heat exchange through air; equipment and materials behave differently.

factors.label: Radiation
factors.target: Direct galactic cosmic rays and solar flares; measured dose about 1.4 mSv/day (Chang'E-4)
factors.why: Shielded shelters and limited work time are needed; this cannot be tested on Earth.

factors.label: Gravity
factors.why: Changes how soil, drilling, walking, loads and dust behave.

factors.label: Permanently shadowed regions
factors.target: Crater cold traps without sunlight for billions of years; temperature can drop to −230 °C and below
factors.earth: The coldest places on Earth reach about −90 °C
factors.why: Earth has nothing even close to the conditions in which the ice is preserved.

factors.label: Polar illumination
factors.target: The Sun stays within about ±1.5° of the horizon (lunar axial tilt 1.54°)
factors.earth: In polar regions the Sun rises to 30–40°, and polar night comes in winter
factors.why: Long shadows and harsh contrast on the Moon are of a completely different kind.

factors.label: Regolith
factors.target: Sharp glassy dust made by micrometeorite impacts, electrostatically charged
factors.earth: Soils are altered by water, wind and organisms
factors.why: Dust damages mechanisms and breathing systems; Earth soil does not imitate this.

factors.label: Day cycle
factors.target: One lunar day lasts ≈29.5 Earth days
factors.why: Changes the thermal regime, power supply and work schedule.

factors.label: Water and life
factors.target: Water as ice in the soil (LCROSS: about 5.6 wt% at Cabeus); no life
factors.why: Earth analogs bring contamination and biological processes that do not exist on the Moon.

mitigations.label: Vacuum and dust
mitigations.text: Thermal-vacuum chambers with regolith simulants (e.g. the anorthosite-based highlands simulant LHS-1).

mitigations.label: Thin atmosphere and radiation
mitigations.text: High altitude lowers pressure only partly and raises the cosmic-ray dose only moderately, so it is a supplement, not a substitute.

mitigations.label: Gravity
mitigations.text: Mechanical suspension and offloading systems, parabolic flights, water immersion.

mitigations.label: Isolation
mitigations.text: Closed missions at stations such as the Haughton–Mars Project, to test crew psychology, resources and procedures in critical situations.

mitigations.label: Water
mitigations.text: Rehearsing ice extraction from permafrost on Devon and Ellesmere as a step towards lunar craters.

site_notes.label: Haughton (Devon), ≈23 km
site_notes.matches: Impact crater in a polar desert, permafrost, low Sun, well-known station for mission rehearsals.
site_notes.mismatches: The rock is carbonate, not anorthosite; there is an atmosphere, plants and liquid water.

site_notes.label: Devon Island plateau
site_notes.mismatches: No craters; the Sun rises to ≈38° and polar night comes in winter.

site_notes.label: Fosheim Peninsula (Eureka, Ellesmere)
site_notes.matches: Massive ground ice, a good test ground for drilling and ice prospecting.
site_notes.mismatches: Much warmer than in the Moon's shadowed craters; the ice is of terrestrial origin.

site_notes.label: Mistastin, anorthosite (Labrador), ≈28 km
site_notes.matches: Target composition closest to the lunar highlands (mostly anorthosite).
site_notes.mismatches: Forest, lake, humid climate; the polar Sun is not reproduced; weathering by water.

site_notes.label: Mistastin, impact melt
site_notes.matches: Breccias and melt rocks similar to Apollo samples.
site_notes.mismatches: Water and weathering alter the rock; there is no space weathering.

moon.sun_note: Numbers in this table (crater diameters, temperatures, Sun elevation) must be checked against the final CSV and the source list.

good_for.label: Impact structures in the right rocks
good_for.text: Mistastin shows how an impact changes anorthosite, and Haughton helps study crater morphology and expedition logistics.

good_for.label: Cold and permafrost
good_for.text: Devon and Ellesmere give realistic low-temperature conditions for equipment and people.

good_for.label: Ground ice
good_for.text: Fosheim and permafrost valleys allow testing drilling, radar sounding and ice extraction methods.

good_for.label: Lighting geometry with long shadows
good_for.text: On a polar plateau, though the Sun stands higher above the horizon than on the Moon.

moon.conclusion: The similarity ranking shows which Earth site is closest to a lunar reference in temperature, relief, ice, composition and illumination. It does not claim that the site fully reproduces the Moon. Vacuum, radiation and gravity need separate test stands and chambers; combining field analogs with laboratory tests gives the most complete picture.
moon.caveat: Check all numbers against sources before submission and add links without the utm_source parameter.
